Trippin'
TRIP-in
verb (Gen X slang)
From trip (Middle English trippen, to step lightly; to stumble). The 1960s counterculture used trip for an LSD experience and tripping for being under the drug’s influence. By the late 1980s, African-American and hip-hop speech had turned trippin’ into "overreacting, acting irrationally, losing perspective" — "You trippin’!" — with no drug in view, and the phrase ran through 1990s rap, film, and school hallways; don’t trip meant "don’t worry about it."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"You trippin’" is the Gen X way of telling a friend he has lost his head: he is overreacting, imagining things, making a scene over nothing. "Why you trippin’ over a parking ticket?" The word’s history deserves a father’s attention: it was borrowed from the drug culture of the 1960s, where a trip was a mind taken out of itself by a chemical. By the time Gen X used it, it simply meant a mind taken out of itself by emotion. Scripture prizes the opposite. "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). "Be sober, be vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Pro 14:29), and "he that ruleth his spirit" is better "than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). James turns it into a rule for the hallway: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). The old meaning of trip — to stumble — is the honest one: the young man who flies off the handle has tripped over his own temper. But Christ is "able to keep you from falling" (Jud 1:24). A father can use the word gently: son, when you feel yourself trippin’, stop and pray before you speak; the sound mind is a gift God gives, not a mood you have to manufacture.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X / hip-hop slang (late 1980s) for overreacting or acting irrationally, from the 1960s drug trip; Scripture prizes the sound mind (2Ti 1:7) and the man slow to wrath (Pro 14:29).

TRIPPIN’, v. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, African-American and hip-hop speech) Overreacting; acting irrationally; imagining things; losing one’s cool. "Calm down — you trippin’."

Also trippin’ over (fussing about), don’t trip (don’t worry about it); from 1960s trip, a drug experience.

Companions: buggin’, flippin’ out, freakin’ out.

Webster 1828: TRIP, v.i. To stumble; to strike the foot against something, so as to lose the step and come near to fall; or to stumble and fall. 1. To err; to fail; to mistake; to be deficient. …

Decode for parents: "you trippin’" means "you’ve lost your head"; teach the sound mind God gives (2Ti 1:7).

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:7 — "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind."

1Pe 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

Pro 14:29 — "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly."

Pro 16:32 — "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city."

Jas 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Modern Corruption

Trippin’ borrows the drug culture’s picture of a mind taken out of itself; Scripture calls for a sober, sound mind ruled by the Spirit, not by the passion of the moment.

expand to see more

A word from the drug culture. The trip of the 1960s was a deliberate unhinging of the mind, sought as a doorway to experience. By the 1990s the drug had dropped out of the word, but the picture remained: a mind that has slipped its moorings. That the slang was needed at all says something — a generation wanted a word for the person ruled by his own passions. Scripture names the remedy: be sober, be vigilant (1Pe 5:8), because the adversary hunts the unguarded mind.

Ruling the spirit. The Bible does not tell a young man never to feel anger or alarm; it tells him to rule them. He that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city (Pro 16:32). The Christian’s sound mind (2Ti 1:7) is not cold self-control but trust: a heart at rest in God has less reason to trip. When a friend says "you trippin’," a humble believer can take it as a brother’s rebuke and be slow to wrath (Jas 1:19).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English trippen (step lightly, stumble) → 1960s drug trip → late-1980s hip-hop trippin’ (overreacting) → mainstream; Scripture: a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).

Biblical remedy: slow to wrath (Pro 14:29); a sound mind (2Ti 1:7)
